question.problem:
Consider the change of variables given by the matrix equation

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} \\ {y}_{2}\end{aligned}],
$$

and the curve $C,$ defined as

$$
C:\,24{x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+21{x}_{2}^{2}-\sqrt{5}{x}_{1}+2\sqrt{5}{x}_{2}=-\frac{5}{16}.
$$

 

Given that the change of variables above reduces $Q(x)=24{x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+21{x}_{2}^{2}$ to its canonical (diagonal) form $25{y}_{1}^{2}+20{y}_{2}^{2},$ what type of a quadratic curve is defined by $C?$
question.worked_solution:
First, we note the following:

$$
C:\,{{24{x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+21{x}_{2}^{2}}_{⏟}}_{Q(x)}-\sqrt{5}{x}_{1}+2\sqrt{5}{x}_{2}=-\frac{5}{16}
$$

Let's write the given change of variables explicitly:

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} \\ {y}_{2}\end{aligned}]\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}=\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}{y}_{1}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}{y}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}{y}_{1}+\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}{y}_{2},\end{aligned}
$$

We know that the given change of variables reduces $Q(x)$ to its canonical form. Therefore, performing the change of variables on $C,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}24{x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+21{x}_{2}^{2}-\sqrt{5}{x}_{1}+2\sqrt{5}{x}_{2} & =-\frac{5}{16} \\ 25{y}_{1}^{2}+20{y}_{2}^{2}-\sqrt{5}(\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}{y}_{1}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}{y}_{2})+2\sqrt{5}(\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}{y}_{1}+\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}{y}_{2}) & =-\frac{5}{16} \\ 25{y}_{1}^{2}+20{y}_{2}^{2}+5{y}_{2} & =-\frac{5}{16} \\ 5{y}_{1}^{2}+4{y}_{2}^{2}+{y}_{2} & =-\frac{1}{16}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we complete the square for the variable ${y}_{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}5{y}_{1}^{2}+4{y}_{2}^{2}+{y}_{2} & =-\frac{1}{16} \\ 5{y}_{1}^{2}+4({y}_{2}^{2}+\frac{1}{4}{y}_{2}) & =-\frac{1}{16} \\ 5{y}_{1}^{2}+4({y}_{2}^{2}+\frac{1}{4}{y}_{2}+\frac{1}{64}-\frac{1}{64}) & =-\frac{1}{16} \\ 5{y}_{1}^{2}+4({y}_{2}^{2}+\frac{1}{4}{y}_{2}+\frac{1}{64})-\frac{4}{64} & =-\frac{1}{16} \\ 5{y}_{1}^{2}+4({y}_{2}+\frac{1}{8})^{2}-\frac{1}{16} & =-\frac{1}{16} \\ 5{y}_{1}^{2}+4({y}_{2}+\frac{1}{8})^{2} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, performing the change of variables

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{z}_{1}={y}_{1}, \\ {z}_{2}={y}_{2}+\frac{1}{8},\end{aligned}
$$

we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}5{z}_{1}^{2}+4{z}_{2}^{2} & =0 \\ \frac{{z}_{1}^{2}}{\frac{1}{5}}+\frac{{z}_{2}^{2}}{\frac{1}{4}} & =0 \\ \frac{{z}_{1}^{2}}{(\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}})^{2}}+\frac{{z}_{2}^{2}}{(\frac{1}{2})^{2}} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

 

A sum of squares is equal to zero if and only if each summand is zero, so the given quadratic equation represents a single point.
